title: John F. Kennedy International Airport
description: International airport serving New York City
wiki_lead:
John F. Kennedy International Airport (IATA: JFK, ICAO: KJFK, FAA LID: JFK) is the primary international airport serving the New York metropolitan area. It is located on the southwestern shore of Long Island, in Queens, New York City, bordering Jamaica Bay. It is the busiest of the three airports in the New York airport system and the sixth-busiest airport in the United States. The airport, which covers 5,200 acres (2,104 ha), is the largest in the New York metropolitan area. Nearly 100 airlines operate from JFK Airport, with nonstop or direct flights to destinations on all six permanently inhabited continents.
JFK Airport is located in the Jamaica neighborhood of Queens, 16 miles (26 km) southeast of Midtown Manhattan. The airport features five passenger terminals and four runways. It is primarily accessible by car, bus, shuttle, or other vehicular transit via the JFK Expressway or Interstate 678 (Van Wyck Expressway), or by train. JFK is a hub for American Airlines and Delta Air Lines as well as the primary operating base for JetBlue. The airport is also a former hub for Braniff, Eastern, Flying Tigers, National, Northeast, Northwest, Pan Am, Seaboard World, Tower Air, and TWA.
The facility opened in 1948 as New York International Airport and was commonly known as Idlewild Airport. The airport was renamed John F. Kennedy International Airport in late 1963 in tribute to President Kennedy following his assassination earlier in the year.

History


Construction
What would become known as John F. Kennedy International Airport opened in 1948 as New York International Airport though it was commonly known as Idlewild Airport (IATA: IDL, ICAO: KIDL, FAA LID: IDL) after the Idlewild Beach Golf Course that it displaced. It was built to relieve LaGuardia Field, which had become overcrowded after its 1939 opening. In late 1941, mayor Fiorello La Guardia announced that the city had tentatively chosen a large area of marshland on Jamaica Bay, which included the Idlewild Golf Course as well as a summer hotel and a landing strip called the Jamaica Sea-Airport, for a new airfield. Title to the land was conveyed to the city at the end of December 1941. Construction began in 1943, though the airport's final layout was not yet decided upon.
About US$60 million was initially spent with governmental funding, but only 1,000 acres (400 ha) of the Idlewild Golf Course site were earmarked for use. The project was renamed Major General Alexander E. Anderson Airport in 1943 after a Queens resident who had commanded a Federalized National Guard unit in the southern United States and died in late 1942. The renaming was vetoed by Mayor La Guardia and reinstated by the New York City Council; in common usage, the airport was still called "Idlewild". In 1944, the New York City Board of Estimate authorized the condemnation of another 1,350 acres (550 ha) for Idlewild. The Port of New York Authority (now the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey) leased the Idlewild property
grok_lead: John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), located in Jamaica, Queens, in New York City, is the primary international airport serving the New York metropolitan area and one of the busiest airports in the world. Spanning approximately 5,000 acres, it functions as a major gateway for transatlantic, trans-Pacific, and Latin American flights, handling over 90 airlines and serving as the busiest U.S. airport for international passenger traffic. Owned and operated by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, JFK recorded 63.3 million passengers in 2024, helping Port Authority airports achieve a record 145.9 million passengers overall and contributing significantly to the regional economy through 158,000 jobs and $36 billion in annual sales. The airport's history dates back to its dedication on July 31, 1948, as New York International Airportâcommonly known as Idlewild Airportâon a site originally used as a golf course and seaplane base. It was renamed John F. Kennedy International Airport on December 24, 1963, shortly after the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, honoring his legacy as a symbol of American progress and global connectivity. From its inception, JFK was designed to accommodate the post-World War II boom in commercial aviation, featuring innovative architecture like the iconic TWA Flight Center (now a hotel) and serving as the arrival point for historic events, including the Beatles' first U.S. tour in 1964. JFK's infrastructure includes four runways arranged in two parallel pairs, totaling nearly nine miles in length, equipped with instrument landing systems (ILS) for all-weather operations and supporting a wide range of aircraft from narrow-body jets to large wide-bodies like the Boeing 747. The airport currently operates five passenger terminalsâ1, 4, 5, 7, and 8âconnected by the AirTrain system for seamless intra-airport travel, with Terminal 4 serving as a key hub for international carriers like Delta Air Lines and Emirates. It also features extensive cargo facilities, handling over 1.6 million tons of freight annually, underscoring its role as a vital node in global supply chains. In recent years, JFK has undergone a transformative $19 billion redevelopment program, funded by a mix of public and private investments, aimed at modernizing facilities and enhancing passenger experience by 2030. Key projects include the construction of a new 23-gate Terminal 1 (opening in 2026), a $4.2 billion Terminal 6 to replace aging structures, and expansions to Terminals 4 and 8, adding over 4 million square feet of space, sustainable features like electric ground support equipment, and improved amenities such as expanded retail and cultural exhibits. These upgrades address historical criticisms of congestion and outdated infrastructure while positioning JFK as a world-class gateway, with early phases already delivering new gates and roadway improvements in 2025.
